references.text: Eldad and Medad prophesied in the camp, and Joshua asked Moses to stop them. Moses replied that he wished all the Lord's people were prophets. The parallel is clear: Joshua wanted to stop those who were not part of the 'official' group, just as John wanted to stop someone casting out demons without following the disciple group.

Markus' parallel account where John tells Jesus that they tried to stop a man who was casting out demons in Jesus' name because he did not follow them. Jesus answers that whoever is not against them is for them.
Jesus' response to John's objection in this passage: 'Whoever is not against you is for you' – the direct continuation of the conversation in verse 49.

Jesus says: 'Whoever is not with me is against me.' This presents an apparent contradiction to 9:50 and clarifies that context determines meaning – here it concerns being neutral toward Jesus himself, while 9:49-50 deals with other believers acting in his name.

The sons of Sceva tried to cast out evil spirits in Jesus' name without having a genuine relationship with him. This contrasts with the man in Luke 9:49 who actually succeeded in casting out demons in Jesus' name, indicating that he had genuine faith.

Paul writes that no one can say 'Jesus is Lord' except by the Holy Spirit. This supports that the man who cast out demons in Jesus' name acted by the Spirit's power, even though he did not belong to the disciple group.

Paul rejoices that Christ is preached, regardless of motive or circumstances. This reflects the principle in Luke 9:49-50: what matters is that God's work is done in Jesus' name, even if it happens outside the established circle.
The seventy return with joy and say that even demons are subject to them in Jesus' name. This shows that Jesus' name has power to cast out demons, the same theme as in 9:49.
